questions.q: What is a monolith?
questions.explain: The Task API is a monolith: every feature runs in one process. That is simple to run and debug, and most successful products started this way.
options: An application that is always badly written
One program with one codebase, deployed as one unit
Many small services that talk over the network
A database with only one table

questions.q: According to the lesson, when does a monolith become a problem?
questions.explain: Being one program is fine. The trouble is a "big ball of mud", where every part can touch every other part and a change in one place breaks something far away.
options: As soon as it has more than one file
When it runs on more than one CPU core
When the code grows and nothing stops one part from reaching into another part's data
When it uses a database

questions.q: The orders code changes the catalog's data directly. What does this print?
questions.explain: Nothing checks the rule "you cannot sell what you do not have", because the orders code changed the stock itself. The rule belongs to the catalog, and it was skipped.
options: Error: Only 2 mug left

questions.q: What do developers mean by a big ball of mud?
questions.explain: In a ball of mud, a harmless-looking function in one folder (like a Black Friday price change) can break rules owned by another part of the app.
options: A program with too many comments
Code where every part can touch every other part's data, so nobody can tell what depends on what
A program split into too many services
A database that has no indexes

questions.q: What is a modular monolith?
questions.explain: From the outside it is one app. Inside, each module owns one business area, exposes a small public API and owns its data.
options: Several programs deployed separately, one per module
Still one program and one deployment, but split inside into modules with hard edges
A monolith that loads plugins from npm
A monolith without a database

questions.q: A module owns one area of the business, like catalog or orders. What is such an area called?
questions.explain: In ShopFlow, catalog (products and stock), orders (carts and checkout), users and payments are separate bounded contexts, and each becomes a module.
options: A layer
A domain boundary, or bounded context
A microservice
A schema migration

questions.q: Which list shows good module boundaries?
questions.explain: Draw boundaries around business areas, not technical layers. Controllers, services and utils are folders inside a module.
options: controllers, services, utils
catalog, orders, payments
small-files, big-files
get-routes, post-routes

questions.q: In a modular monolith, what is shared by all modules?
questions.explain: Infrastructure is shared; only the data and the rules are split. Sharing one database server is fine, sharing tables between modules is not.
options: The database tables
Each module's private files
The infrastructure: logger, configuration, event bus, database connection and HTTP server
Nothing at all: each module has its own server

questions.q: The orders module needs an answer right now: "is this product in stock?". Which way of talking fits?
questions.explain: A direct call to the public API is right when you need an answer. Events are for "something happened". Reading another module's tables or private files breaks the boundary.
options: Publish an event and wait for someone to answer
Call the catalog's public API
Read the catalog's products table directly
Import the catalog's private feature file

questions.q: An order was placed, and the e-mail, analytics and loyalty modules may care. How should orders tell them?
questions.explain: If orders called every interested module, it would depend on all of them, and one slow module would slow every checkout. With an event, orders does not even know who listens.
options: Call each of the three modules one by one
Publish an order.placed event that any module may subscribe to
Write a row into each module's tables
Send them the orders module's private data

questions.q: What may other modules use from the catalog module?
questions.explain: index.ts is the module's public API. Everything else, such as the features/ folder, is private. Every export is a promise you have to keep, so keep the API small.
options: Any file in the catalog folder
Only what the catalog's index.ts exports on purpose
The catalog's database tables, read-only
Everything, as long as it is TypeScript

questions.q: zudojs generate module catalog printed "Could not register the module in app.ts automatically". What should you do?
questions.explain: In CLI 2.0.1, a fresh modular monolith's app.ts has no module list yet, so the generator cannot add it for you. Import the modules and put them in the map yourself.
options: Nothing: the runtime finds modules by itself
Run the command again until the warning disappears
Add the module to the modules passed to createRuntime in src/app.ts by hand
Delete the module and create it again

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The Map lives inside the function. The returned object only has the two methods, so no other code can reach the products directly: that is the module's hard edge.
options: undefined [ 'getProduct', 'reserve' ]

undefined [ 'products', 'getProduct', 'reserve' ]
TypeError: catalog.products is not a function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: getProduct returns a new object built with spread (...). Changing that copy does not touch the catalog's own data; the only way to change stock is through the catalog's API.
options: undefined
TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'stock'

questions.explain: The only way to change stock is reserve, and reserve checks the rule. After the first reservation 1 mug is left, so asking for 3 is refused and the stock stays 1.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The catalog checks its own input and throws a NotFoundError from @zudojs/errors, which carries status 404. Callers get a clear error instead of a crash deep inside.
options: NotFoundError 404 No product hat
TypeError undefined Cannot read properties of undefined
NotFoundError 400 No product hat
Error 500 No product hat

questions.q: What is the composition root?
questions.explain: Modules do not create each other. The composition root wires them together, for example by registering each module's API in the container under a token the module exports.
options: The first module the runtime starts
The one place (like app.ts) that creates every module and hands each one what it needs
The root folder of the git repository
The module with the most dependencies

questions.q: TypeScript refuses catalog.products on a CatalogApi. Why is that still not enough to protect the boundary?
questions.explain: Types are a strong fence, but a deep import skips the public API. The team rule is: import another module only through its index.ts, checked by a test or a lint rule.
options: TypeScript errors are only warnings
A developer can still import a private file like ../catalog/features/catalog.feature.js directly
TypeScript does not check interfaces
Types are removed only in production

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Another module's index.js is its public API, so it is allowed. Files inside the same module are allowed too. Only the deep import into the catalog's private features folder is refused.
options:
null
orders may not import catalog/features/catalog.feature.js
null

null
null
null

orders may not import catalog/index.js
orders may not import catalog/features/catalog.feature.js
null

null
orders may not import catalog/features/catalog.feature.js
orders may not import orders/features/orders.feature.js

questions.q: ShopFlow gets a PostgreSQL database. How does each module keep owning its data?
questions.explain: Sharing one database server is shared infrastructure, which is fine. Sharing tables between modules is what turns them back into a ball of mud.
options: Each module gets its own database server
One schema per module, like catalog.products and orders.orders, and only that module's code touches its schema
All tables go in one schema, and every module may read all of them
Modules store their data in the event bus

questions.q: An order page shows the product and its price. What should the orders module do?
questions.explain: No joins across modules. A copy taken at checkout also says what the customer really paid, even if the product is renamed or repriced later.
options: Join orders.orders with catalog.products to get the current name and price
Store the sku and the price it charged, a copy taken at checkout time
Read the catalog's tables once per request
Ask the customer to type the price again

questions.q: The order keeps a copy of the price. What does this print?
questions.explain: The order stored numbers, not a link to the catalog. A later price change, even to 0, does not rewrite what the customer paid.

questions.q: Two modules subscribe to order.placed, and analytics has a bug. What does this print?
questions.explain: In its default CONTINUE mode, the bus runs every handler and collects failures in the result. The e-mail is still sent, and one broken module does not break checkout.
options:
notifications: e-mail ada@example.com
handlers: 2 ok: 1 failed: 1
Error: analytics database is down

notifications: e-mail ada@example.com
handlers: 2 ok: 2 failed: 0
handlers: 2 ok: 0 failed: 2

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each failure in result.errors wraps the handler's error as its cause. Log them: a failure nobody sees is a failure nobody fixes.
options: logged: analytics database is down
logged: undefined
Error: analytics database is down
logged: order.placed

questions.q: No module subscribes yet. What does this print?
questions.explain: Publishing an event nobody listens to is not an error. Orders does not know or care who listens; a loyalty module can subscribe later without any change to orders.
options: Error: no handler for order.placed

questions.q: Why does the order.placed event carry the email and sku, not just the order id?
questions.explain: An event should carry what its subscribers need. Then the notifications module can send the e-mail without importing or calling the orders module.
options: Events must always be large
A subscriber that had to call back into orders to learn more would be coupled to orders again
So the event can be used as a database row
The event bus refuses small events

questions.q: Where does the OrderPlacedEvent definition belong?
questions.explain: The module that publishes an event owns its definition and exports it from index.ts. Subscribers import only that definition, never the orders code.
options: In the notifications module, which uses it
In the orders module's public API, because orders publishes it
In every module, copied once per subscriber
In the database

questions.q: The event bus lives in memory. The process crashes right after the order is saved and before the event is handled. What happens, and what is the fix when that matters?
questions.explain: Memory is gone after a crash. Inside one app that is often acceptable. When it is not, the outbox pattern stores the event with the order, so it can be published later.
options: The bus replays the event on restart automatically
The e-mail is never sent; save the event in the same transaction as the order and publish it afterwards (the outbox pattern)
The order is deleted automatically
Nothing is lost, because memory survives a crash

questions.q: In @zudojs/cqrs, what is the difference between a command and a query?
questions.explain: Separating writes from reads makes each one's intent clear, and lets every write pass through one bus where middleware can log, time or check it.
options: Commands are sync, queries are async
A command changes something (PlaceOrder); a query only reads (GetProduct)
Commands are sent to all handlers, queries to one
Queries can only return strings

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The orders handler asks the catalog by the query name only. The middleware is on the command bus, so it sees PlaceOrder but not the query, without either module doing anything.
options:
audit: PlaceOrder
{ total: 36 }
{ total: 36 }

audit: PlaceOrder
{ total: 60 }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: No module registered a CancelOrder handler, so the bus throws at once. The sender learns clearly that nobody handles this command.
options: CommandHandlerNotFoundError
undefined
NotFoundError
TypeError

questions.q: Two modules both register a handler for PlaceOrder. What does this print?
questions.explain: A command has exactly one owner. Registering a second handler throws, and the first one stays in place.
options:
DuplicateHandlerError
orders module
checkout module
orders module

DuplicateHandlerError
checkout module

questions.q: What does sending every write through one command bus give a monolith?
questions.explain: Middleware on the bus sees every command without any module doing extra work. That is where an audit log belongs.
options: It makes every command run in parallel
Logging, timing and permission checks can wrap all writes in one place, as middleware
It removes the need for a database
It turns the monolith into microservices

questions.q: Should every call between modules go through a command or query bus?
questions.explain: Do not put everything through a bus by reflex. CatalogApi.getProduct(sku) is clear and simple. Reach for commands and queries when they add something.
options: Yes, always: direct calls are forbidden
No: a plain interface call is easier to read and test; use the bus when you want its middleware or want modules to share only message names
Yes, because buses are faster than function calls
No: buses are only for tests

questions.q: OrdersModule declares dependencies: ["catalog"] and is listed first. In which order does the runtime start and stop the modules?
questions.explain: The runtime starts a module after the modules it depends on. On shutdown the order is reversed, so orders stops using the catalog before the catalog goes away.
options: Start orders, catalog; stop orders, catalog
Start catalog, orders; stop orders, catalog
Start catalog, orders; stop catalog, orders
In the order they are listed, both times

questions.q: Why is a modular monolith a good way to prepare for microservices?
questions.explain: If a module only talks through its public API, events and commands, those calls can later cross the network. If it reaches into other modules' tables, there is nothing clean to cut along.
options: Because it already uses the network between modules
A module with a clean edge can later be moved into its own service; a tangled one cannot
Because microservices need exactly one database table
It is not: you must start with microservices

questions.q: When should you move a module into its own service?
questions.explain: A modular monolith gives you most of the order of microservices without the network problems. Stay in one process as long as you can.
options: As soon as the module has more than three files
Right away, because microservices are always better
Only with a concrete reason, such as a very different load or a separate team
Never: a service can never be split out

questions.q: You add inStock(sku) and orders checks it before reserve. Why must reserve still check the stock itself?
questions.explain: inStock is a quick check for a nicer message. The rule must live in the one place that changes the stock, which is reserve.
options: It does not need to; inStock is enough
Between the inStock check and reserve, another request may buy the last item
Because inStock is slower than reserve
So that reserve can be removed later

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first loop reserves the only mug. The second time, inStock is false, so the loop prints sold out and skips reserve.

reserved 1
sold out

reserved 1

questions.q:
Finish reserve in the catalog: throw a ConflictError with the message Only <stock> <sku> left when the quantity is more than the stock; otherwise lower the stock. The program should print:

ConflictError Only 1 mug left
1
questions.explain: The rule "you cannot sell what you do not have" lives in the one function that changes the stock. Check first, then change, so a refused order leaves the stock as it was.

questions.q: Finish placeOrder in the orders module. Use only the catalog API it receives: get the product, call catalog.reserve, then store and return { id, sku, quantity, total } with id counting from 1. The program should print { id: 1, sku: 'tee', quantity: 2, total: 40 }.
questions.explain: The orders module never touches the products Map; it cannot even see it. It asks through getProduct and reserve, so the catalog's rules always run.

questions.q: Add an inStock(sku) method to the catalog API: it returns true when the stock of that sku is more than 0. Unknown skus count as 0. The program should print true false false.
questions.explain: The new method reads the private Map and returns only a boolean. Other modules learn what they need and nothing more.

questions.q:
Add a loyalty subscriber to order.placed: give one point per unit bought, keep a running total per e-mail in points, and print loyalty: <email> has <n> points. Do not change the publishing code. The program should print:

loyalty: ada@example.com has 2 points
loyalty: ada@example.com has 5 points
questions.explain: A new module joins by subscribing. The orders code, which publishes the event, did not change at all.
questions.expected:
loyalty: ada@example.com has 2 points
loyalty: ada@example.com has 5 points

questions.q:
After publishing, print logged: <message> for every failed handler, using error.cause.message of each item in result.errors. The program should print:

notifications: e-mail sent
logged: analytics database is down
questions.explain: The bus keeps checkout working when one subscriber fails, but it cannot fix the subscriber. Logging result.errors makes sure somebody sees the failure.
questions.expected:
notifications: e-mail sent
logged: analytics database is down

questions.q: The catalog module must answer the GetProduct query. Register a handler on queries that returns { sku, price }, with the price from prices (0 when unknown). The program should print { total: 40 }.
questions.explain: The orders handler only knows the query name GetProduct and the shape of its answer. The catalog owns the prices and answers the query; the two modules share nothing but message names.

questions.q: Finish placeOrder so each order stores a copy of the unit price at checkout, as unitPrice, plus the total. A later price change must not change old orders. The program should print { sku: 'mug', quantity: 2, unitPrice: 12, total: 24 }.
questions.explain: Storing the price the customer paid means no join to the catalog is needed later, and the order stays true after the price changes.
